Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. As a result, LITT patients can receive more effective treatment evaluations with minimal invasiveness.

Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. The code and datasets are available for public access at https://github.com/zhou2019/CE.

Multiple methods for state reconstruction require different data processing steps, and the resulting distributions might appear complex and hard to interpret, especially when trying to analyze rapid dynamics or subtle effects. In an effort to simplify the analysis of such dynamics by leveraging the relationship between state representation and observable properties, we review how changes in entanglement and the onset of synchronization in the dynamics of sub-systems can be identified from their tomograms without needing full state reconstruction. This review aims to demonstrate how distribution patterns in specific tomographic plots directly indicate variations in certain non-linear functions of the sub-systems' statistics and, consequently, in certain quantum correlations. This knowledge should be particularly useful for future experiments seeking to investigate rapid dynamics and subtle effects in complex quantum systems. Furthermore, due to the generality of our analysis, which applies to any system with a pair of sub-systems, we also anticipate its utility in research on other areas of quantum physics, particularly in examining non-local effects, testing quantum metrics, and investigating system behavior in different quantum states. Besides, we include a set of practical exercises to guide physicists in applying these findings to their own experimental data.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers have found these problems to be intriguing, yet they have not been resolved. In this paper, we take the topological approach to defining angle functions and provide solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, we explore additional outcomes, including a demonstration that the embedding of spaces with angle functions is not dependent on the cardinality of the underlying space's distance metric, and we establish a connection between the embedding's dimension and the nature of the angle function.
